title: A shopping cart that never says no
teaches: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, replicas along the ring, quorums (N, R, W), hinted handoff, and Merkle-tree repair
summary: **Design around the primary availability requirement.** Amazon designed Dynamo so that customers could always add items to their shopping carts, even during server, disk or network failures.
**Many points per server.** With one point on the ring, a dead server's keys all land on one neighbour; with a hundred points they spread over every server.
**Replicate each key across N servers.** A key's preference list consists of the first N distinct physical servers encountered walking clockwise from the key's position on the ring.

**Configure R + W > N for overlapping quorums.** A write waits for W replica acknowledgements and a read waits for R replica responses; when R + W exceeds N, every read quorum shares at least one replica with every strict write quorum.

**Use partial quorums to reduce tail latency.** Waiting for 2 of 3 replicas prevents the slowest replica from delaying the request, whereas setting R + W to N or less trades read freshness for lower latency and higher availability.
**A sloppy quorum keeps writes flowing.** A copy meant for a dead server goes to the next healthy one with a hint, and is handed back when the server returns.

**Synchronize diverged replicas with Merkle trees.** During background anti-entropy, two replicas compare hash trees from the root downward to isolate and transfer only the specific key ranges that differ.

**High write availability creates conflicting versions.** Without a leader to serialize operations, two replicas can accept concurrent writes to the same key, requiring the client application to merge divergent versions on read (covered in Lesson 13).
**The name outlived the design.** DynamoDB (2012) has a leader for each partition; the 2007 design lives on in Cassandra and Riak.

blocks.text: In October 2007, the Symposium on Operating Systems Principles met at Skamania Lodge in Stevenson, Washington. Giuseppe DeCandia and eight colleagues from Amazon, including Chief Technology Officer Werner Vogels, presented "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store". The paper described a storage system that Amazon had been running for its shopping cart and other services, and it was unusually frank about the guarantees the design gave up.

Amazon's site was built from services. According to the paper, a single page request typically called more than 150 of them. On one peak day of the holiday season, the shopping cart service handled tens of millions of requests, resulting in more than 3 million checkouts. Each service promised its callers a strict latency bound at the 99.9th percentile, such as 300 ms for 99.9% of requests at a peak load of 500 requests a second, because a simple average hides the slowest experiences (which affect customers with the largest carts and histories, just as we saw with fan-out in Lesson 9).

One core requirement in the paper drives the entire architecture: customers must be able to view and add items to their shopping cart even if disks are failing, network routes are flapping, or datacentres are being destroyed by tornados. A refused "add to cart" request is a lost sale, and at Amazon's volume even a few seconds of refused writes a day costs significant revenue. The engineering team called this property being **always writeable**.
Before designing the architecture, we can state the requirements just as we did for TinyURL in Lesson 3:

blocks.title: What the store must do
points: Read and write a value by its key, such as a cart by its cart ID; values are small, under 1 MB.
Accept every write, even while servers, disks or network links between datacentres are failing.
Answer 99.9% of requests within a few hundred milliseconds.
Scale horizontally by adding machines, with symmetrical nodes and no manual data migration by operators.
Out of scope: multi-key transactions, secondary-index queries by anything other than the primary key, and authentication against untrusted machines inside Amazon's internal network.

blocks.text: The second requirement rules out the architectures from the previous lessons. A single primary, such as the primary replica in Lesson 4 or the GFS master, cannot accept writes while it is down and waiting for failover to complete. Consensus protocols, as covered in Lesson 11, reject writes on the minority side of a network partition. Consequently, Dynamo operates without a leader. Any replica of a key may accept a write, which introduces an explicit trade-off: replicas can diverge, and the system must later reconcile conflicting versions.

parts.title: The ring, with many points each

blocks.text: Dynamo assigns keys to servers using consistent hashing, which we met with memcached in Lesson 5. Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circular keyspace, and a key is assigned to the first server clockwise from its position. However, assigning a single point on the ring to each server leaves two problems. First, the key ranges (arcs) are uneven, because placing random points on a circle produces some gaps several times larger than the average. Second, when a server fails, all of its keys shift to the single next server clockwise, doubling that neighbour's load.

To solve this, we assign each physical server many points on the ring, called **virtual nodes** (or tokens in the Dynamo paper). A server assigned 100 virtual nodes manages 100 small key ranges scattered around the circle. Its total load is the sum of 100 random intervals, which closely approaches the statistical average. When that server goes offline, each of its 100 arcs shifts to a different clockwise neighbour, distributing its load evenly across the remaining cluster. If a new server has double the hardware capacity, an operator can assign it twice as many virtual nodes.

Dynamo replicates each key across N servers, known as the key's **preference list**. To build this list, a node walks clockwise around the ring from the key's hash and selects the first N distinct physical servers, skipping any virtual nodes that belong to a physical server already in the list. Amazon typically configured N = 3. The first server in the preference list usually acts as the **coordinator** for a write request, forwarding the write to the remaining N - 1 replicas and collecting their acknowledgements. The coordinator is an operational convenience rather than a strict leader. If the primary coordinator is unreachable or overloaded, another server in the preference list coordinates the request instead. Because there is no single leader, two different coordinators can process concurrent writes to the same key simultaneously.

blocks.caption: Servers placed on a hash ring. The arcs [[C|data]] owns are drawn thick, and the bars show each server's share of the keys against a fair share. [[Key 17|request]] is stored on the first three distinct servers clockwise from it. Take C out to see who inherits its keys.
blocks.task: With at least five servers, give each enough points that the busiest holds at most 1.3 times its fair share.

blocks.text: In the simulation with six servers, assigning 1 point per server leaves the busiest node holding 2.8 times its fair share of keys. Increasing the allocation to 8 points per server reduces the maximum load to 1.3 times the fair share, and 128 points reduces it to 1.1 times. If you take server C offline when each server has 1 point, all of C's keys shift to a single neighbour; with 64 points per server, C's keys distribute across all five remaining servers.

parts.title: How many replies to wait for

blocks.text: With N = 3 copies of every key and no leader to serialize operations, the coordinator for each request must know how many replicas to wait for before replying to the client. Dynamo exposes this trade-off as two configurable parameters per service. The coordinator sends a write to all N replicas and returns success to the client once **W** replicas acknowledge it. Similarly, the coordinator sends a read to all N replicas and returns once **R** replicas respond, passing back the newest version among those R responses. These required subsets of responses are **quorums**: enough replicas to complete the operation without waiting for the entire preference list.

By the pigeonhole principle, when R + W > N, any read quorum of R replicas must share at least one server with any write quorum of W replicas, because the sum of the two subsets exceeds the total number of replicas N. A read request is therefore guaranteed to query at least one replica that received the latest acknowledged write. Conversely, if R + W is less than or equal to N, the R replicas answering a read might not overlap with the W replicas that acknowledged the latest write, and the coordinator can return stale data.

blocks.caption: A put of [[v2|write]] coordinated by A, then a get coordinated by D, with N = 3. The write reaches B late and C later still; C happens to be the quickest to answer D. A [[red|error]] reply carries the old value v1. The switches "B is down" and "Sloppy quorum" take B out and let D stand in for it. Messages move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Play with R = 1 and W = 2 until you see a stale read, then set R + W above 3 and play again.

blocks.text: The paper documents the quorum configurations Amazon services used in production. **N = 3, R = 2, W = 2** was the standard configuration: read and write quorums overlap, and each operation completes as soon as the fastest two of the three replicas respond, preventing a single slow or failed server from increasing request latency. This mitigates tail latency on a small scale, following the math from Lesson 9: if any single replica has a 1% chance of experiencing a latency spike at a given moment, waiting for all three replicas delays roughly 3% of requests, whereas waiting for two out of three delays only 0.03% of requests. A read-heavy service could configure **R = 1, W = 3** to minimize read latency, while a service prioritizing write availability above all else could set **W = 1**, accepting the risk of stale reads.

Even when R + W > N, quorum overlap provides weaker consistency guarantees than a single leader.[^overlap] Two clients can write to the same key concurrently through two different coordinators. Each coordinator can successfully write to W replicas, leaving the overlapping replica with two conflicting versions that neither coordinator saw. Rather than overwriting one version, Dynamo retains both and defers reconciliation to the conflict-resolution mechanisms we will cover in Lesson 13.

parts.title: When a replica's home is down

blocks.text: Suppose server B, one of a key's N = 3 preference-list servers, is unreachable, and the service requires W = 2. A **strict quorum** only counts acknowledgements from the N servers on the key's preference list. Under a strict quorum, the write succeeds if A and C respond, but if two of the three preference-list servers are down, the coordinator must reject the write. Rejecting that write violates our second requirement of remaining always writeable.

To maintain write availability during failures, Dynamo uses a **sloppy quorum**. The coordinator sends a write to the first N healthy servers it encounters while walking clockwise around the ring. When a server in the key's preference list is down, the next healthy server clockwise beyond the preference list accepts the replica in its place. In the diagram above, server D stands in for server B. Server D writes the object to a separate local database along with a [[hint|write]] in the metadata recording that the replica belongs to B, and periodically probes B to see if it has recovered. Once B responds, D forwards the hinted replica to B and deletes its local copy. This recovery mechanism is called **hinted handoff**. Enable "B is down" and "Sloppy quorum" in the interactive figure above to observe this behaviour. Notice that A considers B down solely because A's own RPC requests to B time out. Each server assesses the health of peers independently during normal request routing, periodically retries unreachable nodes, and learns about permanent cluster membership changes via gossip (explained in the next section). Because there is no centralized failure detector, D independently probes B until it can deliver the hint.

Using a sloppy quorum introduces a specific trade-off in read consistency. Because the W servers accepting a write and the R servers answering a read can now be selected from more than N total nodes on the ring, setting R + W > N no longer guarantees that the read and write sets overlap. A read request coordinated among A, B and C can miss a newer version temporarily stored as a hint on D. Dynamo explicitly trades read freshness for write availability to satisfy its core design requirement. Furthermore, Amazon configured preference lists to span multiple datacentres, allowing sloppy quorums and hinted handoff to absorb the failure of an entire datacentre without dropping writes.

Hints can be lost: D can fail before handing B its copy. So replicas also compare notes in the background, a process called **anti-entropy**. Sending every key to compare would move the whole dataset. Instead each server keeps a **Merkle tree** for each key range it holds: the leaves are hashes of small ranges of keys, and each parent is the hash of its two children.

blocks.caption: Two replicas' Merkle trees for the same key range, cut into eight smaller ranges at the leaves. One leaf range holds a newer cart on replica B, so every hash on the path from that leaf to the root differs. Comparing from the root down finds it without touching the six ranges that agree.

blocks.text: Two replicas exchange their roots. If they match, the whole range agrees and they are done, which is the usual case. If not, they compare the children and descend only into the halves that differ, so finding one differing range among a million takes about twenty levels of comparison, and only that range's keys are sent. The cost is that the trees must be recomputed when key ranges move between servers, which, with points placed at random on the ring, happened every time a server joined or left.[^strategy]

Two additional mechanisms keep data and cluster state synchronized. First, whenever a coordinator executes a read and notices that one of the responding replicas returned a stale version, it asynchronously sends the latest version back to that lagging replica; this is called **read repair**. Second, servers track cluster membership and virtual-node placement using a **gossip** protocol. Once every second, each server contacts one randomly selected peer to exchange its local routing table of active nodes and tokens, propagating membership changes across the entire cluster within a few seconds without relying on a central coordinator. Operators triggered node additions and removals explicitly via command-line tools, preventing temporary network glitches from triggering unnecessary data rebalancing.[^seeds]

Naming the trade-off means saying who pays. Here it is the application. Two replicas that accepted different writes during a failure each hold a version of the cart, and Dynamo returns both on the next read and asks the caller to merge them. For the cart, the merge is a union of the items, which keeps every addition and can bring back an item the customer deleted. Lesson 13 is about exactly that. The paper measured how often it happened: over 24 hours of the cart service, 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version.[^versions]

Dynamo also imposed high operational overhead on engineering teams. Service developers had to tune N, R and W for their workload and write custom reconciliation logic to merge conflicting object versions. System operators had to provision clusters manually and manage background load from Merkle-tree recalculations and hinted-handoff queues.

When Amazon Web Services launched **DynamoDB** as a managed cloud service in January 2012, it retained the Dynamo name and the key-value API, but replaced the leaderless architecture. As detailed in a 2022 USENIX ATC paper on DynamoDB, each storage partition is replicated across three availability zones using a single leader elected via Multi-Paxos (the consensus optimization from Lesson 11 that maintains a stable leader across a sequence of writes). All writes and strongly consistent reads route through the partition leader; if the leader fails, the partition pauses writes for a few seconds until the remaining replicas elect a new leader. At the 2012 launch, Werner Vogels noted that relatively few teams inside Amazon had adopted the original 2007 Dynamo system because each team had to operate and tune its own cluster, and application developers disliked writing conflict-resolution code. Teams preferred a fully managed service where a partition leader serializes writes automatically, eliminating divergent versions. Nevertheless, the 2007 leaderless design heavily influenced the wider industry: co-author Avinash Lakshman built Apache Cassandra at Facebook using Dynamo's ring and quorum model,[^cassandra] while Riak and LinkedIn's Voldemort implemented the paper's architecture directly.

blocks.title: The trade, named
points: Requirement: accept every write with predictable 99.9th-percentile latency, even during server and network failures.
Trade-off: sacrifice a single global ordering of writes per key and give up guaranteed linearizable reads.
Cost to applications: client code must tolerate occasional stale reads and implement merge logic to reconcile conflicting versions.
When to use it: choose a leaderless quorum system when rejecting a write costs more than resolving a conflict; otherwise, a consensus-based leader per partition is simpler to build against.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on Dynamo
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A key has N = 3 replicas, and a service uses W = 1 and R = 1. What can happen?
choices: A write is refused whenever any one of the three replicas is down
A read can miss the latest write and return a stale value, since R + W is only 2
A read always waits for all three replicas, so every read is as slow as the slowest replica
items.why: R + W = 2 is not greater than N = 3, so the single replica that answers a read is not guaranteed to be the replica that acknowledged the latest write.

items.ask: Why does Dynamo give each server many points on the ring?
choices: So that a client can find any key's servers without looking at the ring or asking any other server
So each key is copied to more than N servers
So load stays even, and a lost server's keys spread over many others instead of one
items.why: Assigning many small key ranges per server keeps each server's total load close to the average, and ensures that when a server leaves, its ranges transfer to many different neighbours.

items.ask: Which requirement drove Dynamo's design more than any other?
choices: Cart writes must be accepted even during failures
Every read must return the most recent write, even when the replicas sit in different datacentres
The store must answer queries on any attribute, not only the key
items.why: The requirement to remain "always writeable" is the reason Dynamo eliminates leaders, uses tunable sloppy quorums and allows replicas to hold conflicting versions.

items.ask: With a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, what does the system give up?
choices: The ability to accept a write while two of the key's own three servers are down
The promise that a read's replicas overlap the write's, since the write may sit on a stand-in
Ordering: a write held by a stand-in is applied after any later write once handed back
items.why: A read queries the servers in the key's preference list, so it can miss a new version temporarily held on stand-in server D until D completes hinted handoff. If D fails before handing the hint back, background anti-entropy via Merkle trees repairs the missing write.

items.ask: Two replicas of a large key range want to find out which keys differ. What do Merkle trees let them do?
choices: Send every key and version to each other, compressed so the transfer is small
Agree on a leader for the range, which then overwrites the other replica
Compare hashes from the root down and swap only ranges that differ
items.why: If the root hashes match, the entire key range is identical; if they differ, the servers traverse down only the mismatched branches to isolate the specific key buckets that disagree.

items.ask: With N = 3, R = 2, W = 2, how long does a read take?
choices: As long as the second-fastest of the three replicas to answer
As long as the slowest replica, since all are compared
As long as the fastest replica, since one reply is enough to answer once the write quorum W is 2
items.why: The coordinator responds to the client as soon as R = 2 replicas reply, cutting off the tail latency of the slowest third replica, just as we saw in Lesson 9.

items.ask: Amazon's DynamoDB uses a leader for each partition, unlike the 2007 Dynamo. What does that choice buy?
choices: Writes that are accepted on both sides of a network partition, with no pause when a server fails
One order of writes per key and no versions to merge, at the cost of a pause on failover
Lower latency for every write, because the leader acknowledges as soon as it has written its own copy
items.why: A leader orders every write, so there are no conflicts to merge; while it is replaced, its partition cannot take writes.

overlap.title: Overlap is not linearizability
overlap.text: Even a strict quorum with R + W > N does not guarantee linearizability (making the system behave as if there were only a single copy of the data). If two reads execute while a write is still propagating across replicas, the first read might hit a replica that has the new value while the second read hits replicas that still hold the old value. Guaranteeing linearizability in a quorum system requires an additional phase where the reader writes the latest value back to a quorum of replicas before returning it to the client. We will define consistency models formally in Lesson 13.

strategy.title: Equal slices of the ring
strategy.text: The paper describes three ways of placing points. In the first, random tokens per server, a joining server took ranges from many others, and each of them had to scan its store and rebuild its Merkle trees. Amazon moved to a ring cut into a fixed number of equal partitions, with the partitions handed out to servers. Ranges then never change shape, so a partition and its tree can move as one file.

seeds.title: Seeds
seeds.text: Purely random gossip could suffer from logical partitions if two newly started nodes only knew about each other and never contacted the rest of the cluster. Dynamo prevents this by designating a small set of well-known nodes as seeds, configured via static addresses or an external configuration service. Every server periodically gossips with a seed node, ensuring that all nodes swiftly converge on a single cluster membership list.

versions.title: How often carts diverged
versions.text: The paper's figures for the 24 hours: 99.94% of requests saw one version, 0.00057% saw two, 0.00047% saw three and 0.00009% saw four. It adds that most of the divergence came not from failures but from many writers at once, often automated clients.

cassandra.title: Inbox search
cassandra.text: Lakshman and Prashant Malik built Cassandra for Facebook's inbox search and released it as open source in 2008. It took Dynamo's ring, gossip, hinted handoff and tunable quorums and Bigtable's data model and log-structured storage (lesson 10). It resolves conflicting writes by timestamp, last writer wins, which lesson 13 shows can lose a write.
